title: Number lines and absolute value
blurb: Read and place any rational number on a number line, and use absolute value as distance.
question: A vaccine freezer is set to −20°C and the medication fridge to 4°C. On a number line, how far apart are these temperatures, and what does absolute value have to do with it?

teach.body: Formally, a number line places every real number at a point, with values increasing to the right, and the absolute value |a| is the distance from a to 0, so it is never negative: |−5| = |5| = 5. In plain English: the number line tells you which number is bigger (the one farther right), and absolute value tells you how far a number is from zero, ignoring direction.

teach.caption: Every number is less than every number to its right: −3.5 < −1/2 < 2 1/4.

items: Find two labeled numbers and count the SPACES between them, not the tick marks: from 0 to 1 there are 4 equal spaces.
A point on the 3rd tick after 2 is 2 + 3 × 0.25 = 2.75.
Check: 2.75 is between 2 and 3 and closer to 3, matching the picture. ✓

head: Expression
Work
Value
teach.caption: Absolute value bars are grouping symbols: work inside them first.

teach.body: Absolute value measures distance, so the distance between two numbers a and b is |a − b| (order doesn't matter). From −3 to 4: |4 − (−3)| = |7| = 7, which matches counting 3 units to 0 and 4 more. From −8 to −2: |−2 − (−8)| = |6| = 6. A distance is never negative.

teach.caption: A negative number can have the larger absolute value and still be the smaller number.

items: Check: both bars give positive sizes, and 8 is larger, so a small positive answer makes sense. ✓

teach.text: Absolute value slips: |−5| is 5, never −5; |3 − 8| is |−5| = 5, not 3 + 8 = 11; −|−4| is −4 (the minus sign outside the bars stays); and on a number line, count spaces between ticks, not the ticks themselves.

teach.h: Scenario: Jasmine checks the cold chain
teach.body: Jasmine Brooks, a pharmacy intern applying to nursing school, logs a freezer at −20°C and a fridge at 4°C. On a vertical number line, the freezer is 20 units below 0 and the fridge 4 above. Distance: |4 − (−20)| = |24| = 24°C. Check by counting: 20 up to 0, then 4 more: 20 + 4 = 24. ✓ The fridge is 24 degrees warmer.

items: Right is greater on a number line; negatives sit left of 0.
Tick value = (difference between labels) ÷ (number of spaces).
Absolute value = distance from 0, so it is never negative.
Distance between a and b = |a − b|; work inside bars first.

summary: You can now read and place fractions, decimals and negatives on a number line, find the value of each tick mark, and use absolute value as distance from zero and between two points. You can also spot the sign and tick-counting slips the TEAS uses.

A.q: On a number line, the segment from 1 to 2 is divided into 8 equal spaces. Point P is on the 6th tick mark to the right of 1. What number is at P?
A.why: Each space is 1 ÷ 8 = 0.125. Six spaces past 1: 1 + 6 × 0.125 = 1.75 (that is 1 6/8 = 1 3/4).

whyNot.0: 1.6 treats each space as 0.1, as if the segment had 10 spaces.
whyNot.1: 1.625 counts the tick at 1 as the first tick, giving only 5 spaces.
whyNot.3: 1.875 is 7 spaces past 1, one space too far.

A.why: Inside the bars first: 3 − 10 = −7. Then |−8| = 8 and |−7| = 7, so 8 − 7 = 1.

A.q: On a number line, point A is at −4.5 and point B is at 2.25. What is the distance between A and B?
A.why: Distance = |2.25 − (−4.5)| = |2.25 + 4.5| = 6.75. Check: 4.5 units to 0, then 2.25 more.

whyNot.0: 2.25 adds −4.5 and 2.25 and drops the sign: the gap crosses 0, so the two sizes add.
whyNot.1: A distance is an absolute value and cannot be negative.
whyNot.2: 4.5 is A's distance from 0, not from B.

B.q: Which number has the greatest absolute value?
B.why: Absolute values: 6.9, 7.2, 0.8 and 7. The largest distance from 0 is 7.2, so −7.2.

whyNot.3: 7 is the greatest VALUE, but its distance from 0 (7) is less than 7.2.

whyNot.1: −|5| = −5 but |−5| = 5; the minus sign outside the bars stays.
whyNot.3: 7 − 7 = 0 and |0| = 0; the bars don't turn subtraction into addition.

B.q: Point Q is halfway between −1/2 and −1/4 on a number line. What number is at Q?

whyNot.0: −1/8 is half the GAP between the points (1/4 ÷ 2), not the point itself.
whyNot.1: 3/8 has the right size but the wrong sign; both endpoints are negative.
whyNot.2: −3/4 adds the two numbers but forgets to divide by 2.

C.why: Bars first: |−3 − 5| = |−8| = 8 and |−2| = 2. Then multiply: 2 × 4 = 8. Finally −8 + 8 = 0.

whyNot.0: 16 drops the minus sign outside the first bars: 8 + 8.

C.q: A number line from −2 to 2 is divided into 16 equal spaces. Point R is 7 spaces to the right of −2. What number is at R?
C.why: The segment is 2 − (−2) = 4 units long, so each space is 4 ÷ 16 = 0.25. R = −2 + 7 × 0.25 = −2 + 1.75 = −0.25.

whyNot.1: −1.125 uses 2 ÷ 16 = 0.125 per space, measuring the line as 2 units long instead of 4.
whyNot.2: −0.5 counts 6 spaces instead of 7, treating the tick at −2 as the first.
whyNot.3: 1.75 measures the 7 spaces from 0 instead of from −2.

C.q: Two points on a number line are each 3.5 units from −1. What are the two points?

whyNot.0: −2.5 and 4.5 are 3.5 units from +1, not from −1.
whyNot.3: −4.5 is correct, but 3.5 is 4.5 units from −1.

reteach.title: Think of floors in an elevator
reteach.question: A hospital elevator has a parking level at −3 and a cafeteria on 5, with 0 at street level. How does riding between them explain number lines and absolute value?

blocks.h: Up is greater, distance is the ride
blocks.body: Stand the number line up and it becomes an elevator shaft. Higher floors are greater numbers, so 5 > −3 even though the parking level feels "far." Absolute value is how many floors you are from street level: the parking level is |−3| = 3 floors away. The ride from −3 to 5 is 3 floors up to street level plus 5 more: |5 − (−3)| = 8 floors.

items: "How far is it from street level?" Absolute value: |−3| = 3, |5| = 5.

blocks.text: A ride is never "−8 floors long." Distances and absolute values are always zero or positive.

explain.body: On a number line, every number is greater than the numbers to its left. Among negatives, the one with the larger size sits farther left, so it is the least.

test.q: Which number lies farthest to the left on a number line?
test.why: Decimals: −1.72, −1.75, −1.705, −1.667. The largest size among negatives is 1.75, so −1 3/4 is the least and farthest left.

whyNot.0: −1.72 is greater than −1.75 because it is closer to 0.
whyNot.2: −1.705 has more digits but is closer to 0 than −1.75.
whyNot.3: −5/3 ≈ −1.667, the closest of the four to 0, so it is farthest RIGHT.

explain.body: Divide the distance between two labeled points by the number of equal SPACES between them. From 0 to 2 with 5 spaces: 2 ÷ 5 = 0.4 per space.

test.q: On a number line, the segment from 0 to 2 is split into 5 equal spaces. What number is at the 3rd tick mark to the right of 0?

whyNot.1: 0.6 uses 1 ÷ 5 = 0.2 per space, as if the segment were 0 to 1.

explain.body: The distance from 0. Work inside the bars first, then take the size. The result is never negative, but a minus sign OUTSIDE the bars still applies.

whyNot.3: 26 adds the last term instead of subtracting it: 9 + 4 + 13.

explain.body: Distance = |a − b|. If both numbers are on the same side of 0, subtract their sizes; if they are on opposite sides, add their sizes.

test.q: How far apart are −7 and −2 on a number line?
test.why: |−2 − (−7)| = |−2 + 7| = |5| = 5. Both are negative, so subtract their sizes: 7 − 2 = 5.

whyNot.0: 9 adds the sizes, which is right only when the points are on opposite sides of 0.
whyNot.3: 7 is the distance of −7 from 0, not from −2.
